newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS-Norway crown sinks amid market confusion.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Norway crown sinks amid market confusion.

text.p: The Norwegian crown sank to a four-week low on Thursday as foreign exchange markets reacted with confusion to a central bank announcement that it would resume buying foreign currency.
The crown plunged to a low of 4.0340 against the mark, a level last touched on January 24, after trading at an intraday high at 3.969.
Market players said the reaction had been violent and overdone due to confusion over the bank's motives.

Norges Bank, rattled by a an apparently unstoppable surge in the Norwegian currency, announced on January 10 that it would curb massive and fruitless intervention on the foreign exchange market -- a policy it had used to stabilise the crown.
The bank said on Thursday it would resume foreign currency purchases, but not "as exchange market interventions", rather for management of the Government Petroleum Fund.

"It shows the market has a very short memory," said a London-based market player. "Everyone knows it (the bank) has to fulfil purchases for the fund. We're seeing a huge over reaction to a small imbalance in supply and demand."
Others said the bank's announcement looked like a turnaround in policy.
"In January they said they wouldn't intervene and now they say they will. It looks like a reversal in policy and the crown's paying for it," said a dealer.

Oil-rich Norway expects to have a budget surplus of 55.4 billion crowns in 1997, all of which will be placed in the Petroleum Fund for investment. The central bank is charged with converting the amounts into foreign currency and investing overseas.
The bank said that up to January 10, it had bought foreign exchange for 31 billion crowns, leaving 24.4 billion crowns still to be purchased for transfer into the fund.
In addition, foreign currency corresponding to 1.2 billion would be bought and transferred into the government Petroleum Insurance Fund, it said.

"The purchases must be seen against a background of Norges Bank's role as manager of the Petroleum Fund and, as such, the purchases are not undertaken as exchange market interventions," a bank statement said.
One analyst said the bank's January purchases made the crown an even more attract buy because it had already sold more than half of the projected budget surplus for the year.

"The hot money (U.S. funds) saw the headlines and decided to sell Norway in a panic," said one analyst. "We're still positive on the crown. They've sold more than half the surplus and it's only February, the crown is going to be strong all year. You should be buying NOK," she said.
